Empirical Research Plan  
“School Spending, Educational Attainment, and Economic Mobility”

------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Strategy: 2-stage, difference-in-differences (DiD) instrumental-variables (2SLS-DiD).

• Stage 1 (first-stage):  Use the timing of state-level court-mandated school-finance reforms (SFRs) as an instrument for changes in district-level per-pupil spending.  
• Stage 2 (second-stage):  Estimate the causal effect of an additional \$1,000 (2019\$) in per-pupil spending during a student’s K-12 years on (i) completed years of schooling and (ii) log adult earnings.

Why appropriate?  
a. SFR decisions are plausibly exogenous to contemporaneous district economic shocks; they generate large, policy-driven, within-state changes in spending.  
b. The PSID links individuals to childhood school districts and follows them into adulthood, giving long-run outcomes.  
c. A DiD framework absorbs all state-invariant time shocks & constant district differences; instrumenting removes any remaining endogeneity of spending (e.g., reverse causality from unobserved local demand for education quality).

------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
Treated = cumulative real K-12 spending per pupil experienced by individual i in district d and birth cohort c. Operationally:  
Spending_icd = Σ_{k=K to 12} (RealSpend_{d,t=k}) /12, where t indexes grade-year.

Instrument (Z)  
SFR_{s,t} = 1 starting the fiscal year after a state s supreme-court decision that required equalization/adequacy and until another major overhaul. Interact with Pre-reform district poverty gap to capture heterogeneous mandates: Z_{d,t}=SFR_{s,t}×Gap_{d,pre}. This yields larger first-stage variation.

Control group  
Districts in non-reform states during the same calendar years (and districts in reform states in the pre-decision years) serve as counterfactuals.  

Treatment timing  
Event time τ = fiscal year – first reform year. Main DiD specification uses τ≥0 as treated.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Policy exogeneity / exclusion: Conditional on state & year FE, SFR timing is unrelated to unobserved determinants of student outcomes except through spending.  
Plausibility: Court rulings stem from constitutional litigation rather than economic cycles; historical record supports exogeneity.

A2. Parallel trends (in absence of the reform): In the pre-period, outcomes in reform vs non-reform states follow similar trends.  
Plausibility: Reasonable but testable; will examine pre-trends using event-study coefficients.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA):  Reform in state s does not affect students in other states except via observed spending (no cross-state spillovers).  
Plausibility: Some migration, but PSID indicates <4 % cross-state migration while in K-12; robustness checks exclude movers.

A4. Relevance (first-stage strength): SFRs generate sizable increases in per-pupil spending; past evidence suggests F-stat > 20.

A5. Monotonicity (IV): Districts do not decrease spending in response to mandates that require increases (no “defiers”).  
Plausibility: Mandates set minimum funding floors; budgets rarely fall.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  

T1. Concurrent state education policies (e.g., desegregation, Head Start).  
Mitigation:  Add controls for major contemporaneous policies; include state×year covariates for desegregation orders, federal program intensity.

T2. Selective migration of families into higher-spending districts after reforms.  
Mitigation:  (i) Restrict to children residing in the same district for ≥10 of 12 school years, (ii) Use PSID family fixed effects exploiting sibling timing, (iii) Compare results to sample with no post-reform in-movers.

T3. Measurement error in linking students to historical district spending.  
Mitigation:  (i) Use interpolation only when district boundaries unchanged; (ii) Instrumental-variable approach attenuates classical measurement error; (iii) Sensitivity analysis dropping districts with major boundary changes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)   # fast TWFE & IV
library(AER)      # ivreg robustness
library(broom)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge data
psid  <- fread("PSID_students_1955_85.csv")         # individual-level
spend <- fread("District_Spending_1955_85.csv")      # district-year
sfr   <- fread("State_SFR_Timing.csv")               # state-year

# Merge spending to PSID by district & year
psid <- merge(psid, spend, by = c("district_id","year"), all.x = TRUE)
# Merge reform indicator
psid <- merge(psid, sfr, by = c("state","year"))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# Real 2019$ spending (already in spend)
psid[, real_spend := spend_pp_2019]

# Cumulative K-12 exposure for each child
psid[, spend_k12 := mean(real_spend), by = .(person_id)]     # average over grades

# Instrument: SFR × pre-reform poverty gap
psid[, gap_pre := first(poverty_gap), by = .(district_id)]
psid[, sfr_iv  := sfr*gap_pre]

# Outcome variables
psid_final <- unique(psid[, .(person_id, birth_cohort, state,
                              years_schooling, log_earnings,
                              spend_k12, sfr_iv)])

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS regression (cluster at state level)
iv_main <- feols(log_earnings ~ 1 | state + birth_cohort ~ spend_k12 | sfr_iv,
                 data = psid_final, cluster = "state")
summary(iv_main, stage = 1:2)

# Secondary outcome: educational attainment
iv_ed <- feols(years_schooling ~ 1 | state + birth_cohort ~ spend_k12 | sfr_iv,
               data = psid_final, cluster = "state")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: Event-study pre-trend test
psid[, event_time := year - sfr_first_year]
es <- feols(log_earnings ~ i(event_time, ref = -1) | state + birth_cohort,
            data = psid[event_time >= -10 & event_time <= 20],
            cluster = "state")
iplot(es)      # visual parallel-trends check

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Save tidy output
write.csv(tidy(iv_main), "main_results.csv")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS (PRIORS)  

Direction: Positive. Each additional \$1,000 (2019\$) in annual K-12 spending is expected to raise:  
• Completed schooling by ~0.05–0.10 years.  
• Adult log earnings by 1.5 %–2.5 % (≈\$800–\$1,300 in 2019 dollars at median income).

Economic intuition: Higher spending improves class size, teacher pay, and instructional resources, which translate into skill accumulation and higher productivity.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (1 = strong, 0 = weak)

[1] First-stage relevance (F-stat > 10) ............... 1  
[2] Exogeneity of instrument .......................... 0.8  
[3] Parallel pre-trends confirmed ..................... 0.9  
[4] No manipulation of treatment timing ............... 0.9  
[5] Stable sample / no spillovers (SUTVA) ............. 0.75  

Overall, methodology is robust but still vulnerable to unobserved concurrent policies and migration. Carefully executed robustness tests and falsification exercises are essential.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
